title: The Kindly Harvest
premise: Yara Sandoval returns to the family farm to bury her twin brother Yago, only to find the body in the casket wearing her face—and on the porch sits Tam, the imaginary friend they invented as children, unchanged after twenty years. As the harvest moon approaches, Yara learns that the town's founding families made a bargain: every generation must 'invite in' one of their own to be replaced by something that wears their shape. The thing wearing Yago's memories is not her brother but a patient collector, and it has decided this year's kindly harvest is Yara. To survive until sunrise, she must uncover which living neighbor brokered the invitation—her own mother—and choose between exposing a justice the law can't touch or letting the town's old debt be paid. In the end, Yara turns the invitation back on its maker: she names her mother to the thing at the threshold, and at dawn only one twin-shaped figure walks out of the farmhouse, and no one, not even the reader, is certain which.
about_author: Rosalind Villalobos is the pen name of a former agricultural inspector who spent a decade documenting abandoned farmsteads across the borderlands, where locals refused to walk certain fields after dark. She writes horror about inheritance, rural silence, and the bargains families make that outlive them.

chapters.title: The Wrong Face in the Casket
chapters.summary: Yara arrives home for her twin brother's funeral and finds the corpse wearing her own features, down to a childhood scar. The funeral director shrugs; her mother, Elena, won't meet her eyes. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: uncanny dread braided with grief—the first crack in her certainty that nothing here is supernatural.

chapters.title: Tam on the Porch
chapters.summary: That night Yara finds Tam, the imaginary friend she and Yago invented at age seven, sitting on the porch swing exactly as they left him. He speaks only in rules: don't answer the door, don't say your full name, hold out until sunrise. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: vertigo of childhood made real; she refuses to believe even as she obeys.

chapters.title: What the Town Buries Sideways
chapters.summary: At the wake, Yara notices the town's deference to her family is fear dressed as respect. Old farmer Delgado pulls her aside, mentions 'the last harvest' and stops mid-sentence when Elena enters. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: isolation deepens—everyone knows something, and everyone is complicit in the silence.

chapters.title: Yago's Room, Unchanged
chapters.summary: Searching her brother's room for answers, Yara finds his journal: pages of tally marks counting down to the harvest moon, and sketches of Tam drawn before either twin could write. The last entry reads 'It's not me they want.' POV: Yara. Emotional beat: grief curdling into guilt—she left him alone with this.

chapters.title: The Thing That Answers
chapters.summary: Someone knocks past midnight using Yago's knock, his voice, his childhood nickname for her. Yara nearly opens the door; Tam's hand closes over hers through the wood. Through the peephole she sees her brother's face smiling wrong. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: terror sharpened by longing—the cruelest trick is a door that sounds like home.

chapters.title: Delgado's Debt
chapters.summary: Delgado tells Yara the founding-families bargain over whiskey: each generation invites one of their own in, and the land stays generous. His own son was harvested in 1987; he shows her the field where nothing grows. POV: alternating Yara and Delgado. Emotional beat: the horror becomes historical, systemic—power feeding on the powerless.

chapters.title: Mother Knows Best
chapters.summary: Yara confronts Elena, who admits the family owes a debt but insists it isn't what Yara thinks. Elena's hands are stained with chalk—the same chalk marks Yara found under the porch. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: betrayal's first sting; maternal love revealed as possibly the most dangerous thing on the farm.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Tam finally explains the mechanics: an invited guest cannot be refused, but a named host cannot refuse. Sunrise breaks the claim—but only if the invited one never speaks her full name aloud before dawn. POV: Tam, in his strange, literal voice. Emotional beat: fragile hope built on arbitrary rules; the reader learns the game board.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises Early
chapters.summary: Cloud cover breaks a night ahead of schedule; the moon swells red over the fields. Every door in the farmhouse unlocks itself. Yara realizes someone inside moved the timeline up. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the trap springs—helplessness as the safe hours are stolen from her.

chapters.title: Neighbors at the Fence Line
chapters.summary: The townsfolk gather silently at the property edge at midnight, holding lanterns—not to help, but to witness. Delgado among them, weeping, unable to cross. Yara understands justice here is ritual, not law. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: chilling communal complicity; the theme of power enforced by polite consensus.

chapters.title: The Second Twin
chapters.summary: The thing wearing Yago appears inside the house without entering—it was always partly here. It offers Yara a trade: take Yago's place willingly and he goes free. It speaks with intimate knowledge of her worst memory. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: temptation and self-loathing; the monster knows exactly which lever to pull.

chapters.title: Chalk Under the Porch
chapters.summary: Digging beneath the porch, Yara finds decades of chalk circles, each with a name and date—her grandmother's handwriting, then her mother's, then fresh: her own name, dated tomorrow. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: cold confirmation; the invitation wasn't negotiated, it was written, signed, and waiting.

chapters.title: Elena's Confession
chapters.summary: Cornered, Elena confesses: the family chose Yara years ago because she left—absence made her easier to give up than Yago. She believed distance would soften the taking. POV: Elena, in close third. Emotional beat: the villain humanized; corruption justified as protection, love as accounting.

chapters.title: Tam's True Name
chapters.summary: Yara demands to know what Tam really is. He admits he was the previous harvest—a child invited in 1962 who refused to become the collector and has been bound to thresholds ever since, warning each next victim. POV: Tam. Emotional beat: tragic revelation; the imaginary friend was the last person who chose differently.

chapters.title: The Longest Hour
chapters.summary: With two hours to sunrise, the house begins rewriting itself—hallways lengthening, windows showing the 1962 harvest replaying. Yara must navigate a home turned labyrinth while refusing to speak her name. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: endurance horror; identity itself under siege as the house tries to make her forget who she is.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Yara realizes no court, priest, or sheriff will ever touch this—the town's whole legal order exists to protect the bargain. If anyone pays, it will be by her hand and her naming. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: resolve crystallizing; the theme lands—justice must be seized where institutions are the crime.

chapters.title: The Naming
chapters.summary: At the threshold, Yara speaks—not her own name, but Elena's full name, the true host who wrote the invitation. The collector turns from her toward the woman who signed the debt. Elena screams that a mother can't be harvested by her own child. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: climax—liberation and damnation in a single breath.

chapters.title: What the Collector Takes
chapters.summary: The collector accepts the naming but reveals the price: a host must be given freely, and Yara's naming counts as giving. Tam intervenes, offering himself as the freely-given one, dissolving fifty years of threshold-binding into one final act. POV: alternating Yara and Tam. Emotional beat: sacrifice as the only clean currency left.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn floods the farmhouse. The collector, holding Tam's small hand, steps backward into the field where nothing grows, and the ground closes like water. The neighbors disperse without a word, lanterns snuffed. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: hollow victory; survival that feels like loss.

chapters.title: Two Funerals
chapters.summary: Yara buries the casket properly—inside it now, chalk dust and her mother's wedding ring. Elena is gone, unmentioned, unmourned publicly, erased the way the town erases everything. Yara signs the death certificate with a steady hand. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: grim closure; justice rendered leaves no one clean.

chapters.title: The Field Where Nothing Grows
chapters.summary: Before leaving, Yara walks Delgado's barren field and plants something there—an act of defiance against land fed on blood. The soil takes it. Somewhere behind her, faintly, a child laughs on a porch. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: tentative healing shadowed by ambiguity; the cycle may be broken, or merely paused.

chapters.title: Kindly
chapters.summary: Driving away, Yara passes a new family moving onto the old Delgado farm, their daughter waving at someone in the empty passenger seat. Yara keeps driving, then doesn't—she turns around, because staying invisible was never really an option. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: bittersweet final note; she chooses witness over escape, carrying the truth forward.
